TEMPORARY ROAD LANE CLOSURE IN BATASAN/COMMONWEALTH AVE. (EASTBOUND)

Pansamantalang isasara ang apat na lane sa gitnang bahagi ng eastbound ng Commonwealth Avenue mula Amity Street hanggang Ilang-Ilang Street simula 11 PM ngayong gabi, April 1, 2026 hanggang alas-4 ng madaling araw bukas, April 2, 2026, ayon sa inilabas na traffic advisory ng Department of Transportation (DOTr).

Bahagi ng unloading at lifting works ng elevators at escalators para sa Metro Rail Transit Line 7 ang nasabing pansamantalang road closure, ayon sa DOTr.

Samantala, mananatiling bukas at madaanan pa rin ang dalawang lane ng service road habang isinasagawa ang nasabing aktibidad.

COURTESY: Department of Transportation/Facebook

Bisitahin ang https://t.co/bAMF9JO2Xs para sa updates.

THE GULF AFTER THE WAR

Oil markets closed March on their biggest monthly gain since 1988. This morning Brent trades near $101 after Trump said the US military will leave Iran in two to three weeks. No deal required. The price dropped. The architecture underneath did not.

The war did not create the Gulf's power problem. It exposed it. Thirty years of American deterrence papered over deep structural fault lines. Those fault lines are now visible. Whatever replaces the old arrangement will not be built in Washington.

I. The Security Guarantee Repriced

Trump's Truth Social post telling countries to go get their own oil was the first signal. His Oval Office statement last night was the second. "We leave because there's no reason for us to do this." Two thirds of Americans want the war over quickly, even if US goals are not achieved. (Reuters/Ipsos) Domestic pressure, not strategy, is now driving the exit timeline.

For thirty years, US military presence in the Gulf was unconditional. Basing rights. Patriot batteries. The Fifth Fleet in Bahrain. Gulf states paid with oil priced in dollars, arms purchases, and political alignment. That deal has become both time-limited and transactional.

Every Gulf capital is asking the same question: what does the base agreement actually buy us when Washington can declare victory and leave, whether or not Hormuz is open?

II. Saudi Arabia's Four-Dimensional Play

MBS is playing multiple boards at once. Hosting US forces. Maintaining the defence pact with Pakistan. Keeping back channels open with Iran through Oman and China. Positioning Saudi as the swing producer the world cannot function without.

Saudi's 2025 defence budget hit $78 billion, 21 percent of total government spending. (GAMI) Localisation at 19 percent and rising. THAAD components now produced domestically. Baykar TB2 agreements signed with Turkey. The war has accelerated Saudi's defence industrial base by at least a decade.

With 38 percent of Hormuz crude flows, Riyadh holds more structural leverage than at any point since 1973. The real question is whether MBS can turn temporary leverage into lasting architecture before oil prices normalise.

III. UAE vs Saudi: The Rivalry the War Made Visible

Abu Dhabi and Riyadh are nominally allies and structurally competitive. UAE built the most diversified Gulf economy, the most aggressive overseas investment posture, and the most sophisticated intelligence apparatus in the region.

The war hit UAE harder precisely because of that centrality. Fujairah struck seven times. Dubai Mall footfall down 24 percent. (Dubai Tourism Authority) Real estate down 4 to 5 percent. (DLD, March 2026) Hotel bookings collapsed. The bypass infrastructure made UAE indispensable and therefore a target.

Abu Dhabi wants this war over faster than Riyadh does. MBS has higher tolerance for elevated prices and prolonged conflict. That divergence is real even if not publicly admitted.

When Saudi signed the defence pact with Pakistan in September 2025, MBZ visited India almost immediately. That timing was not coincidence. UAE is quietly building its own parallel network, one that does not require deference to Riyadh's vision of Gulf leadership.

IV. Qatar and Bahrain: The Vulnerability of Small States

Qatar hosts the largest US air base in the Middle East and Hamas political leadership simultaneously. Israel struck Doha in September 2025. QatarEnergy declared force majeure on LNG exports after the Hormuz closure. The base agreement did not prevent the economic damage.

Bahrain hosts the Fifth Fleet and has a Shia majority population with historical ties to Iran. Kuwait's airport struck by Iranian drone last night. Small states in a fragmenting security environment pay first and get consulted last.

V. STEP: Signalling or Real Alliance?

The Saudi-Pakistan defence pact was signed September 2025. Turkey pushing for membership. Egypt aligned but unsigned. Four foreign ministers met in Riyadh on March 19. Dar flew to Beijing on March 30. Wang Yi and Dar called for an immediate ceasefire the following day. (Reuters, April 1) The architecture is producing diplomatic output faster than anyone expected.

UAE is conspicuously absent. Qatar is hedging. Kuwait is silent. GCC as a bloc has not embraced it. Pakistan remains on IMF life support. Turkey's involvement makes Gulf monarchies nervous. The Belfer Center called the nuclear dimension political signalling, not operational commitment.

STEP works as a hedge against American unreliability. It is unlikely to function as a serious offensive alliance capable of deterring Iran independently. Alliances built under fire, before real trust exists, tend to fracture once the pressure eases.

VI. Real Power: Equipment vs Will to Use It

Saudi's $78 billion defence budget has not stopped years of Houthi attacks. UAE has advanced air defences and strong intelligence. Neither has shown sustained offensive capability against Iran without US support.

The deeper issue is dependency. Gulf air forces run on American platforms requiring American spare parts, software updates, and political approval for offensive operations. The F-15 that defends Riyadh cannot strike Tehran without Washington's green light. That is not a military limitation. It is a political one baked into the procurement relationship.

Diversifying defence procurement away from the US is now the active conversation in every Gulf capital. The war created the political space for it. That shift takes a decade. It started this year.

VII. China and India

China is the only power running a profit on every outcome. Bought 1.38 million bpd of Iranian oil in 2025 at an $8 to $10 discount. (Kpler, Columbia CGEP) Still moving 1.22 million bpd through a partially closed strait. Holds 1.2 billion barrels in strategic reserves. (The Diplomat) Released diesel to Philippines and Vietnam this weekend despite its own export ban. Called for ceasefire in Beijing today. Iran is the discount window. The Arab bloc is the 50-year investment horizon. Beijing is running both simultaneously and is now on record as the peace broker.

India holds the most relationships across this conflict's fault lines of any Asian power. 8 million workers in the Gulf. Over $100 billion in annual remittances. Ties with Iran, Israel, the US, and Gulf states simultaneously. That remittance architecture is quiet leverage most analysis does not price. The diplomatic lane narrowed in the short term. The structural leverage does not disappear. It waits.

VIII. The Fragmented Gulf

The Gulf in five years will not be dominated by any single power. Saudi holds swing producer leverage. China holds energy client and ceasefire broker leverage. US retains military presence but with declining credibility. Iran retains chokepoint leverage. UAE holds financial and logistics hub leverage. Turkey holds its NATO bridge role. Pakistan holds nuclear signalling value and active mediation role. India holds remittance and labour leverage it has not yet converted into diplomatic capital.

None strong enough to dictate outcomes alone. All strong enough to veto outcomes they oppose.

The war will end. Brent will fall. The underlying architecture the war exposed will not be rebuilt. It will be negotiated around, hedged against, and exploited by whoever moves fastest in the gap between what was and what comes next.

The price dropped this morning. The structural problem did not.
